title: Identifying interstitial lung disease with large language models on clinical notes and claims
authors: Larghero, G.; Schneeweiss, S.; Gu, B.; Anand, P.; Lin, J. K.; Yang, J.
abstract: BackgroundInterstitial lung disease (ILD) is a potentially fatal toxicity of immune check-point inhibitors and antibody-drug conjugates. Drug-safety studies in healthcare databases identify ILD with claims-based algorithms that trade positive predictive value (PPV) against sensitivity. We assessed whether large language models (LLMs) improve on these algorithms, with and without electronic health record (EHR) notes, and whether these gains translate into measurable epidemiological benefits. MethodsIn 309 oncology patients with ILD diagnosis codes at Mass General Brigham, adjudicated by two pulmonologists, we compared 12 open-access LLMs with 20 published claims-based algorithms. LLMs received claims, EHR notes, or both, without task-specific training. Measures were PPV and yield (proportion classified positive). We projected the attenuation of a drug-induced ILD odds ratio under non-differential outcome misclassification. FindingsLLMs extended the PPV-yield frontier of the published algorithms with all three inputs. Across the 36 model-input evaluations, LLM PPV exceeded that of the best algorithm without specialist-coding requirements (Algorithm 4) by 14.3 percentage points on average. With claims alone, Qwen3-8B achieved 89.8% PPV (95% CI 78.2-95.6) at 15.9% yield, versus 86.7% at 4.9% for the highest-PPV algorithm. With notes alone, Qwen3-32B achieved 78.9% PPV at 49.2% yield, versus 64.6% at 51.1% for Algorithm 4. With combined claims and notes, Qwen3-14B achieved 100.0% PPV at 24.3% yield. Under a simulated drug-safety scenario with a true odds ratio of 3.0, the projected observed odds ratio was 2.67 with combined inputs versus 1.07 with Algorithm 4, corresponding to a 46-fold difference in the estimated sample size required for 80% power (591 versus 27,200 patients). InterpretationZero-shot LLMs offer a higher-PPV alternative to rule-based claims pheno-typing for ILD, on all three input types. Because the claims-only configuration uses the same claims data as existing algorithms, it could be deployed in administrative databases without linked notes, and may recover drug-safety signal otherwise lost to outcome misclassification. FundingNational Institute on Aging, National Library of Medicine, PCORI, and the National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed up to August 2026 for studies on claims or electronic health record (EHR)-based identification of interstitial lung disease and on machine-learning or large language model (LLM) phenotyping of clinical conditions. Search terms included "interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis", "administrative claims", "computational phenotyping", "rule-based algorithms", "machine learning", and "large language models". We also screened the reference lists of relevant articles. The literature search suggested that identifying ILD in longitudinal claims data is unreliable because the relevant diagnosis codes are nonspecific, and validated rule-based algorithms face a structural tradeoff between PPV and coverage. Supervised machine-learning classifiers have outperformed rule-based ILD identification on electronic health record data, and zero-shot LLMs have already shown the ability to phenotype chronic conditions from structured codes. No study, however, had compared a zero-shot LLM head-to-head against validated, published claims-based algorithms for a specific, high-stakes drug-safety outcome on a single fixed cohort, isolated the contribution of the input substrate from that of the model, or quantified the downstream consequence for pharmacoepidemiologic effect estimation. Added value of this studyOn a single, fixed, expert-adjudicated cohort, the evaluated LLMs achieved higher positive predictive value (PPV) than all 20 published claims-based algorithms at comparable yield (the proportion of patients classified as ILD-positive), whether the models received structured claims, clinical notes, or both. Across the 36 model-input evaluations, PPV exceeded that of the most inclusive published rule by 19.7 percentage points on average, and did so in 33 of 36 evaluations. We show that clinical notes generally increased yield, while the resulting PPV-yield trade-off depended on the model and input combination. Restricting the input to a single EHR note type preserved the advantage over rule-based phenotyping in matched comparisons on the patients possessing that EHR note type. Most consequentially, this improvement reduces the sample size required to detect a hypothesised drug-ILD association from approximately 27,200 patients for the best existing algorithm for the task to 591 when using LLMs, and offer a deployable upgrade for the note-free administrative databases where rule-based algorithms are the current standard. Implications of all the available evidenceFor pharmacovigilance of treatment-related ILD, the limiting step is often not the size of the available claims database but the misclassification that erodes the very signal under surveillance. Replacing rule-based claims phenotyping algorithms with zero-shot LLM-based alternatives transforms a high-PPV, low-yield classifier into one that recovers many more patients at the same PPV, converting a classifier that can render drug-safety associations statistically invisible into one that makes them detectable in cohorts of feasible size. Pending external validation, this offers a practical route to more sensitive post-marketing surveillance of the pulmonary toxicity of immune checkpoint inhibitors and antibody-drug conjugates. More broadly, we hypothesise that this advantage is not specific to ILD: zero-shot LLM phenotyping may recover drug-safety signal for other outcomes that diagnosis codes capture poorly but that are well documented in clinical text, a possibility that warrants dedicated evaluation.

infographic.key_insight: Zero-shot LLMs improved the trade-off between positive predictive value (PPV) and positive classification yield for interstitial lung disease compared with published claims-based algorithms.
infographic.clinical_relevance: More accurate ILD identification could strengthen drug-safety research, including in claims databases without linked clinical notes.
method: Evaluated 12 open-access LLMs using claims, EHR notes, or both, without task-specific training.
Compared performance with 20 published claims-based algorithms using pulmonologist-adjudicated ILD status.
Projected drug-safety effect estimates and sample-size requirements under simulated outcome misclassification.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 309 oncology patients with ILD diagnosis codes, claims-only Qwen3-8B achieved 89.8% PPV at 15.9% yield, versus 86.7% PPV at 4.9% yield for the highest-PPV claims algorithm.
infographic.watch_item: Evaluation was limited to code-positive oncology patients at one health system; epidemiological benefits were simulated rather than demonstrated in a drug-safety study.
infographic.paper_title: Identifying interstitial lung disease with large language models on clinical notes and claims

title: Findings-aware Language-Image Pretraining for CT Volume Interpretation
authors: Takuro Shimaya, Junya Inoh, Masahiro Saiko
abstract: Computed tomography (CT) provides diverse patient information and various clinical tasks, for which numerous deep learning models have been investigated. Recent years have seen the development of vision-language foundation models that can comprehensively extract clinical features, driven by representation learning that combines CT volumes with radiology reports. Existing approaches typically adopt Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP)-based representation learning, where pairs from different cases are, in principle, treated as negative pairs such that the volume and report embeddings are pushed apart. In the biomedical imaging, however, treating different cases as negative pairs is not always appropriate, particularly when clinical similarity exists. In this study, we propose a supervised representation learning framework grounded in clinical knowledge from language foundation models, rather than the weak supervision used in CLIP. Specifically, we utilized a large language model to extract abnormal finding phrases from reports. We then explicitly constructed the target features that the image encoder should output, as the semantic representation of the extracted findings using a biomedical text embedding model. Our Findings-aware Language-Image Pre-training (FiLIP) outperformed weakly supervised approaches in multi-label zero-shot finding classification in both in-domain and external-domain evaluations, and also proved effective when fine-tuned for the downstream task of radiology report generation.

infographic.key_insight: FiLIP trains CT representations using report-derived abnormal findings, avoiding the assumption that different patient cases should always be pushed apart.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support CT finding recognition and radiology report generation, but clinical utility remains unestablished.
method: Use a large language model to extract abnormal finding phrases from radiology reports.
Encode those findings with a biomedical text embedding model to construct target representations.
Train a CT image encoder to predict these finding-based representations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports better multi-label zero-shot finding classification than weakly supervised approaches in in-domain and external-domain evaluations, plus benefits for fine-tuned report generation, without numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Errors or omissions in report-derived findings could propagate into training targets; the abstract does not describe extraction validation.
infographic.paper_title: Findings-aware Language-Image Pretraining for CT Volume Interpretation

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Heterogeneous Cognitive and Biomedical Knowledge Graphs: The Role of Graph Grounding in Multi-Hop Reasoning and Hallucination Mitigation
authors: Ali Sarabadani, Kheirolah Rahsepar Fard, Tahereh Jeirani
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in biomedical and cognitive neuroscience, but their ability to reason reliably over heterogeneous knowledge graphs (KGs) remains unclear. We benchmark five LLMs (GPT-5.1, Gemini 2.0 Pro, Llama 3, Qwen, and BioGPT) across five KGs: DrugBank, NeuroSynth, Cognitive Atlas, Brain Map, and GDPKG. We introduce a multitier query dataset to evaluate reasoning depth and factual accuracy under KG-aware (graph-grounded) and KG-agnostic conditions. Inter-annotator agreement was substantial, with Cohen's kappa of 0.781 (range: 0.753-0.807) and Fleiss' kappa of 0.77. Results show that general-purpose models, particularly GPT-5.1 and Gemini 2.0 Pro, generally outperform domain-specific models on multi-hop and high-level reasoning tasks, although performance declines as query complexity increases. KG grounding reduces hallucination rates across all evaluated models. Contrary to our initial hypothesis, domain-specific models do not consistently outperform general-purpose models on specialized tasks without graph grounding. These findings highlight the value of combining broad language-model capabilities with structured domain knowledge. We provide practical guidance for selecting LLM-KG integration strategies based on task complexity and computational constraints, and discuss hybrid neurosymbolic architectures for personalized medicine, cognitive disorder diagnosis, and explainable AI.

infographic.key_insight: Graph grounding reduced hallucinations across all five evaluated LLMs, while general-purpose models generally outperformed domain-specific models on complex reasoning tasks.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Combining LLMs with structured biomedical knowledge may improve research tools, but this benchmark does not establish safety or effectiveness in patient care.
method: Benchmarked GPT-5.1, Gemini 2.0 Pro, Llama 3, Qwen, and BioGPT.
Used DrugBank, NeuroSynth, Cognitive Atlas, Brain Map, and GDPKG.
Compared graph-grounded and graph-agnostic performance on multitier reasoning and factual-accuracy queries.
infographic.evidence_signal: Annotation agreement was substantial (Cohen’s κ = 0.781; Fleiss’ κ = 0.77), and model performance declined as query complexity increased.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no numerical effect sizes for hallucination reduction and reports no clinical validation.
infographic.paper_title: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Heterogeneous Cognitive and Biomedical Knowledge Graphs: The Role of Graph Grounding in Multi-Hop Reasoning and Hallucination Mitigation

title: Multidimensional Suicide Risk Assessment with Machine Learning using Electronic Health Records
authors: Nathan Scollar, Kemal Davaslioglu, Nathan Conger, Sastry Kompella, Yalin E. Sagduyu, Nathaniel D. Bastian
abstract: Suicide prevention remains a critical public health challenge, and electronic health records (EHRs) provide an opportunity to characterize suicide-related risk indicators using documented clinical, behavioral, medical, and social-contextual information. This paper presents a multidimensional machine learning framework to model and estimate suicide-related outcomes using MIMIC-IV EHR data. We construct clinically motivated diagnosis categories and define a composite outcome from documented codes corresponding to suicidal ideation, suicide attempt, prior suicidal behavior, and intentional self-harm. To address severe class imbalance and reduce age-related confounding, we apply age-matched resampling that retains all positive patients and samples comparison-cohort patients from the same age group. Logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost classifiers are evaluated before and after resampling with isotonic calibration. The calibrated XGBoost model achieves the strongest matched-cohort performance, outperforming the other evaluated classifiers. SHAP-based interpretation shows that diagnostic burden, depression-related features, age, personality-disorder history, social determinants related to violence, and medical comorbidity contribute to elevated predicted probabilities. Our results demonstrate that combining broad EHR-derived features, age-matched cohort construction, calibration, and feature-level interpretation provides a practical framework for retrospective suicide-related risk modeling.

infographic.key_insight: Calibrated XGBoost performed best among the evaluated models for classifying documented suicide-related outcomes in an age-matched EHR cohort.
infographic.clinical_relevance: EHR-derived clinical and social-contextual features may support suicide-related risk research, but these findings do not establish readiness for clinical screening.
method: Used MIMIC-IV diagnosis categories to define features and a composite suicide-related outcome.
Retained all positive patients and age-matched comparison patients to address imbalance and reduce age confounding.
Compared logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost with isotonic calibration; used SHAP for interpretation.
infographic.evidence_signal: In retrospective MIMIC-IV evaluation, calibrated XGBoost showed the strongest matched-cohort performance; the abstract reports no numerical metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Code-based outcomes capture documented events, not necessarily future risk; external validation and evaluation at real-world prevalence are needed.
infographic.paper_title: Multidimensional Suicide Risk Assessment with Machine Learning using Electronic Health Records

title: Learning a patient world model for health system simulation in intensive care
authors: Yingtai Li, Ruoyan Wang, Yu Li, Shaohua Kevin Zhou
abstract: Designing healthcare strategies requires anticipating their clinical and operational consequences before implementation, a task that often relies on health system simulation. Such a simulation necessitates modeling how patient states evolve and generate care demands. However, conventional approaches typically tailor compact state transitions to a single policy question and omit history-dependent dynamics, thus requiring the redefinition of states and transitions when there is a new question that entails different clinical information. We propose to learn a patient world model from longitudinal EHRs using a neural network to provide a shared clinical representation of patient trajectories that can serve simulation questions across scenarios. Taking ICU operations as an example, we train the model on MIMIC-IV, freeze it, and couple its time-queryable predictions to shared ICU calendars, resources, and queues via scenario-specific mappings, so that one model renders admission demand, care tasks, and discharge proposals across simulations evaluating ICU bed capacity, care dispatch, and post-ICU transfer capacity. Experiments show that our model matches Markov and semi-Markov comparators in aggregate occupancy and directional responses to capacity and dispatch policies. It also reproduces policy gains from replayed observed trajectories. For patients entering the same support state from different prior trajectories, the learned representation captures a 24-h recovery difference (-6.4 predicted versus -6.7 observed percentage points), a contrast missed by compact state models, which propagates into distinct simulated care demand, queue burden, and bed use. These results indicate that a learned world model of patient dynamics has the potential to replace question-specific state models, allowing new care policies to be evaluated by reconfiguring the scenario without model rebuilding.

infographic.key_insight: A learned patient world model could support multiple ICU planning simulations without rebuilding patient-state models for each policy question.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could help health systems explore how ICU bed capacity, care dispatch, and post-ICU transfer capacity affect care demand and resource use before implementation.
method: Train a neural patient-trajectory model on longitudinal MIMIC-IV electronic health records.
Freeze the model and connect its time-queryable predictions to shared ICU calendars, resources, and queues.
Adapt scenario-specific mappings to simulate different operational policies.
infographic.evidence_signal: In simulation evaluations, the model matched Markov and semi-Markov comparators on aggregate occupancy and directional policy responses, while capturing a history-dependent 24-hour recovery contrast of −6.4 percentage points versus −6.7 observed.
infographic.watch_item: Simulation agreement does not establish real-world operational benefit; validation beyond MIMIC-IV and prospective evaluation remain important.
infographic.paper_title: Learning a patient world model for health system simulation in intensive care

title: NPCBench: A Clinical Apprenticeship Benchmark for Multimodal Care-Pathway Reasoning in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
authors: Pengkai Wang, Wei-Wei Zhang, Yan Li, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Zeyu Liu
abstract: Current medical benchmarks typically break down clinical competence into isolated factual questions, single-image tasks, or static case vignettes. These tests score individual answers, but reveal less about whether a model can integrate subspecialty knowledge with multimodal evidence and track a patient's condition throughout a course of care. To close this gap, we introduce NPCBench, a clinical apprenticeship benchmark for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). NPCBench mirrors specialist training, from guideline and foundational knowledge to case planning, longitudinal review, CarePath integration, and open-ended consultation. It contains 4,777 component and consultation items and a 100-patient CarePath cohort with 417 scored diagnostic and care tasks. The episode-level evaluation tests whether diagnostic and care answers are jointly correct within a care pathway. By linking stepwise tasks to patient-level care trajectories, NPCBench evaluates whether models ground decisions in visual evidence, interpret changes in patient state, and meet clinical requirements in consultation. Across 30 evaluated models, we observe a composition gap: strong performance on individual tasks does not ensure jointly correct diagnostic and care answers for the same patient. Among 21 multimodal models, strict CarePath success reaches at most 23%. Paired controls and physician calibration further examine evidence grounding, longitudinal revision, and consultation judging. Overall, NPCBench broadens the evaluation of medical artificial intelligence beyond static question-answering paradigms to an apprenticeship-oriented assessment of clinical workflows, thereby offering a testbed for evidence-based and temporally coherent reasoning in oncology care.

infographic.key_insight: Strong performance on isolated medical tasks did not ensure jointly correct diagnostic and care answers across a patient's nasopharyngeal carcinoma care pathway.
infographic.clinical_relevance: NPCBench tests capabilities relevant to oncology workflows, including visual evidence use, longitudinal reasoning, and integrated care planning.
method: Models specialist apprenticeship from foundational knowledge to case planning and consultation.
Links multimodal, stepwise tasks to patient-level care trajectories.
Uses episode-level scoring, paired controls, and physician calibration.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation covered 30 models, 4,777 component and consultation items, and 100 CarePath patients with 417 scored tasks; strict CarePath success peaked at 23% among 21 multimodal models.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark performance does not establish safety or effectiveness in real-world clinical care.
infographic.paper_title: NPCBench: A Clinical Apprenticeship Benchmark for Multimodal Care-Pathway Reasoning in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma

title: How Deep is the Signal? Time-Context up to 30 Years for Colorectal Cancer Prediction in a Primary-Care EHR Model
authors: Achille Raviez, Lan Wang, Brendan Delaney
abstract: EHR foundation models read medical events within a fixed context window, and long context has so far been measured only in tokens. How far back in time a model must look to capture the earliest predictive signal is unknown. We introduce time-context, the calendar lookback window before the prediction point, and provide, to our knowledge, the first systematic evaluation of decade-scale time-context for an EHR foundation model. We pretrained a decoder-only transformer (34.6M parameters) on 1.4B coded events from 3.6M primary-care patients in North West London and fine-tuned it to predict incident colorectal cancer under a 12-month pre-diagnostic buffer. A frozen cohort of 1,008 cases and 9,582 matched controls, all registered for at least 30 years, was evaluated at 15 nested lookback windows from 2 to 30 years, so that every truncation is compared within the same patients. Discrimination rose from an AUROC of 0.551 at 2 years to 0.590 at 18 years, then plateaued, with about 80% of the gain reached within 10 years; an XGBoost baseline converged to the same level (peak AUROC 0.589). A simulation further suggests that rotary position embeddings (RoPE) over elapsed time alias beyond about 20 years at the default base frequency, motivating a retuned $θ$. Time-context is a measurable design axis for clinical prediction models, distinct from token-context, and should be reported.

infographic.key_insight: Colorectal cancer prediction improved with longer EHR lookback, reaching about 80% of the observed AUROC gain within 10 years and plateauing around 18 years.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Historical primary-care records may add predictive information, but the modest discrimination does not establish clinical utility.
method: Pretrained a 34.6M-parameter decoder-only transformer on 1.4B coded events from 3.6M patients.
Fine-tuned for incident colorectal cancer prediction with a 12-month pre-diagnostic buffer.
Compared 15 nested lookback windows spanning 2–30 years within the same cohort and against XGBoost.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 1,008 cases and 9,582 matched controls registered for at least 30 years, transformer AUROC rose from 0.551 at 2 years to 0.590 at 18 years; XGBoost peaked at 0.589.
infographic.watch_item: Findings from patients with at least 30 years of registration in one UK region may not generalize to populations with shorter or fragmented records.
infographic.paper_title: How Deep is the Signal? Time-Context up to 30 Years for Colorectal Cancer Prediction in a Primary-Care EHR Model

title: Variantscape: Retrospective Study of Large Language Model-Based Extraction of Variant-Treatment-Cancer Associations from Published Oncology Abstracts
authors: Wosny, M.; Blindu, A. S.; Boesch, M.; Peres, T.; Niederhauser, T.; Fruh, M.; Rothermundt, C.; Hastings, J.
abstract: ObjectivesPrecision oncology relies on accurate interpretation of tumour-detected gene variants, to guide personalised treatment decisions. However, interpretation of variants in context requires extensive information that is often buried within unstructured biomedical literature and obscured by inconsistent nomenclature, making manual retrieval labour-intensive and prone to omissions. In this study, our aim was to evaluate the potential of large language models to extract variant-treatment-cancer associations at scale from published abstracts. DesignWe developed Variantscape, a large-scale, automated pipeline and open-access web tool. It integrates traditional natural language processing methods with state-of-the-art large language models to extract, standardise, and analyse co-associations between genetic variants, cancer types, and therapeutic interventions from published biomedical abstracts. ResultsFrom over 3.7 million abstracts published between January 2014 and October 2026, 886,195 articles containing gene names were eligible for extraction. Among these, 37,895 (4.3%) mentioned a variant, cancer type, and therapeutic agent together, covering 11,985 unique variants across 197 cancer types and 547 therapeutic agents. LLM verification against the abstract text confirmed at least one association in 35,224 papers, giving a literature-derived graph of 10,571 nodes and 44,644 verified edges. Canonical alterations in well-studied cancers (e.g., BRAF V600E in melanoma) were strongly linked to established treatments, while several rare variants also emerged with high-confidence literature support. ConclusionsBy applying large language models to biomedical literature, Variantscape enables scalable, context-aware extraction of trilateral variant-treatment-cancer relationships. This approach supports early evidence synthesis/hypothesis generation, highlights underrecognized or rare associations for MTB preparation, and offers a practical resource for accelerating discovery and supporting precision oncology research and translation. FundingThis study was funded by the School of Medicine at the University of St. Gallen in Switzerland under grant number 2300380. Article SummaryO_ST_ABSStrengths and limitations of this studyC_ST_ABS[bullet] Variantscape combines traditional natural language processing with large language models to enable scalable, automated extraction of variant-cancer-treatment relationships from over 3.7 million biomedical abstracts, substantially reducing the manual search burden inherent to existing molecular tumour board workflows. [bullet]The pipeline applies large language model-based inference to standardise inconsistent genetic nomenclature across the literature, improving the comparability and reliability of extracted associations that would otherwise be obscured by terminological variation. [bullet]Variantscape is designed as a continuously updatable, open-access resource, meaning it can incorporate newly published evidence without requiring repeated manual intervention. [bullet]The pipeline relies solely on abstract-level text rather than full-text articles, which may limit the depth and granularity of extracted associations, as key methodological details, variant context, and nuanced clinical findings are frequently reported only within the body of published papers. [bullet]Automated extraction using large language models introduces a risk of misattribution of variant-cancer-treatment relationships, and without systematic manual validation of outputs, the precision of identified associations at scale remains difficult to fully characterise.

infographic.key_insight: Variantscape uses large language models and traditional NLP to extract variant–treatment–cancer associations from oncology abstracts at scale.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The tool may support precision oncology evidence review and molecular tumour board preparation, but extracted associations are not treatment recommendations.
method: Screen biomedical abstracts for gene names.
Extract and standardise variants, cancer types, and therapeutic agents.
Use LLMs to verify associations against abstract text and build a literature-derived graph.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 886,195 eligible abstracts, 37,895 (4.3%) mentioned all three entity types; LLM verification identified at least one association in 35,224 papers, yielding 44,644 verified graph edges.
infographic.watch_item: LLM verification against abstracts does not establish clinical validity; the abstract reports no independent expert-validation accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Variantscape: Retrospective Study of Large Language Model-Based Extraction of Variant-Treatment-Cancer Associations from Published Oncology Abstracts

title: MedGraph: Maintaining Patient State with Graph Memory for Long-Term Medical Dialogue
authors: Donghua Zhang, Zizheng Wang, Ze Dong, Yiding Feng, Siyu Qian
abstract: LLM-based medical assistants that follow a patient across visits need a memory that keeps the patient's clinical state correct as it changes. We examine the errors of five memory systems on longitudinal medical dialogue and find three recurring causes: the retrieved evidence gives an outdated state, includes another person's health facts, or lacks a safety fact the answer depends on. We present MedGraph, a graph memory built for these three cases. Construction extracts dated facts from each session, attributes each fact to the person it describes, and links medication, diagnosis, and measurement records into chains that keep earlier states. Retrieval ranks the patient's chains as units, reads each chain at the time the question asks about, and adds the original dialogue text; a patient profile lists every recorded safety fact with every question. On MedMemoryBench, MedGraph has the highest overall accuracy with both a GPT and a Qwen backbone, 10.5 and 10.4 points above the strongest of five baselines, with efficient memory construction and answering in the GPT setting.

infographic.key_insight: MedGraph uses graph memory to track changing patient information, distinguish whose facts are whose, and keep recorded safety facts available across medical conversations.
infographic.clinical_relevance: More reliable longitudinal memory could help medical assistants avoid answers based on outdated states, another person’s history, or missing safety information.
method: Extract dated, person-attributed facts from each dialogue session.
Link medication, diagnosis, and measurement records into chains that preserve earlier states.
Retrieve patient-specific chains for the requested time, add original dialogue text, and include all recorded safety facts.
infographic.evidence_signal: On MedMemoryBench, MedGraph achieved the highest overall accuracy against five baselines with GPT and Qwen backbones, improving on the strongest baseline by 10.5 and 10.4 points, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark gains do not establish clinical safety; performance still depends on correctly extracting, dating, and attributing patient facts.
infographic.paper_title: MedGraph: Maintaining Patient State with Graph Memory for Long-Term Medical Dialogue

title: CardioLM: A multilingual suite of small language models for the cardiology domain
authors: Manuela-Daniela Danu, Miguel Rodríguez-Ortega, Alberto Becerra-Tome, Pablo Arancibia, Fernando Gallego-Donoso, Lorenzo Pratesi
abstract: Background: Cardiovascular care generates large volumes of clinical free-text documentation in local languages. However, clinical natural language processing (NLP) resources remain concentrated in English, and no existing benchmark is cardiology-specific, multilingual, and broad in entity coverage. Methods: We present two contributions. The first is CardioCCC, a corpus of 508 cardiology case reports originally published in Spanish and extended to Czech, Dutch, English, Italian, Romanian, and Swedish through machine translation, annotation projection, and clinician review, with annotations covering diseases, symptoms, procedures, and medications. The second is CardioLM, comprising CardioBERTa, a set of language-specific encoders obtained by continued pretraining on cardiology and biomedical corpora, and CardioNER, a set of named entity recognition (NER) models fine-tuned on CardioCCC. Results: Cardiology-specific pretraining reduced pseudo-perplexity by up to a factor of eight, yet changed strict span-level F1 by at most 0.04, with benefits concentrated in languages whose backbones lacked biomedical coverage. The jointly trained multilingual XLM-RoBERTa-large models achieved the best strict F1 in nearly every language and entity type, exceeding the strongest monolingual system by up to 0.13 F1. A large share of residual errors concerned boundary detection: relaxed matching recovered 0.10-0.23 F1 for disease, procedure, and symptom, but only 0.01-0.07 for medication. Clinicians rated CardioNER well above a rule- and dictionary-based baseline, with the mean rating across entity types rising from 26% to 73%. Conclusions: Specialty-specific pretraining is not the decisive factor for downstream entity recognition, whereas multilingual joint training yields the strongest results in nearly all settings and a simpler deployment path for multi-country clinical information extraction.

infographic.key_insight: Joint multilingual training delivered stronger cardiology entity recognition than language-specific models, while specialty pretraining had limited impact on strict F1.
infographic.clinical_relevance: CardioLM could support extraction of diseases, symptoms, procedures, and medications from multilingual cardiology documentation.
method: Built CardioCCC from 508 Spanish cardiology case reports, extended to six additional languages through machine translation, annotation projection, and clinician review.
Continued pretraining language-specific encoders on cardiology and biomedical text, then fine-tuned entity recognition models.
Compared language-specific and jointly trained multilingual models using strict and relaxed F1 and clinician ratings.
infographic.evidence_signal: Multilingual models exceeded the strongest monolingual system by up to 0.13 strict F1; mean clinician ratings across entity types rose from 26% for a rule-and-dictionary baseline to 73% for CardioNER.
infographic.watch_item: Performance on translated case reports may not generalize to native-language clinical records, and entity-boundary errors remained common.
infographic.paper_title: CardioLM: A multilingual suite of small language models for the cardiology domain

title: MIMIC-Note-Extract: A Large-Scale Structured Dataset Extracted from MIMIC-IV-Note Discharge Summaries
authors: Kristian Schwethelm, Jonas Kuntzer, Conrad Ketzer, Eva Wende, Moritz Schlager, Daniel Rueckert
abstract: MIMIC is one of the most widely used public hospital datasets for machine learning on electronic health records, yet clinically important information, such as past medical history, allergies, and diagnostic findings, remains confined to free-text discharge summaries. Studies requiring this information must therefore build their own extraction pipelines, duplicating substantial effort across projects. We release MIMIC-Note-Extract (MNE), a large-scale dataset that uses a hybrid extraction pipeline combining deterministic parsing with schema-guided large language model generation to transform 16 sections from 300,720 discharge summaries into structured tables. MNE adds information that has no structured MIMIC counterpart and enriches related tables with broader coverage and greater clinical detail, including 10 times more patient-history entries and medication histories for more than twice as many admissions. Validation by medical doctors confirms extraction accuracy above 92% across sections. Using MNE, we construct a clinical decision-making benchmark for LLM agents, demonstrating how reusable structured representations of clinical narratives reduce data curation effort.

infographic.key_insight: MIMIC-Note-Extract converts free-text discharge summaries into reusable structured data, reducing repeated extraction work for clinical AI research.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The dataset makes patient history, allergies, and diagnostic findings more accessible for research without establishing readiness for clinical deployment.
method: Process 16 sections from 300,720 MIMIC-IV-Note discharge summaries.
Combine deterministic parsing with schema-guided large language model extraction.
Use structured outputs to build a clinical decision-making benchmark for LLM agents.
infographic.evidence_signal: Medical-doctor validation found extraction accuracy above 92% across sections; MNE provides 10 times more patient-history entries and medication histories for more than twice as many admissions as related structured MIMIC tables.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not detail validation sample sizes or error types, limiting assessment of reliability for specific downstream tasks.
infographic.paper_title: MIMIC-Note-Extract: A Large-Scale Structured Dataset Extracted from MIMIC-IV-Note Discharge Summaries

title: Enhanced MRI brain tumor detection using deep learning in conjunction with explainable AI SHAP based diverse and multi feature analysis
authors: Asif Rahman, Maqsood Hayat, Nadeem Iqbal, Fawaz Khaled Alarfaj, Salem Alkhalaf, Fahad Alturise
abstract: Recent innovations in medical imaging have markedly improved brain tumor identification, surpassing conventional diagnostic approaches that suffer from low resolution, radiation exposure, and limited contrast. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is pivotal in precise and accurate tumor characterization owing to its high-resolution, non-invasive nature. This study investigates the synergy among multiple feature representation schemes such as local Binary Patterns (LBP), Gabor filters, Discrete Wavelet Transform, Fast Fourier Transform, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and Gray-Level Run Length Matrix alongside five learning algorithms namely: k-nearest Neighbor, Random Forest, Support Vector Classifier (SVC), and probabilistic neural network (PNN), and CNN. Empirical findings indicate that LBP in conjunction with SVC and CNN obtained high specificity and accuracy, rendering it a promising method for MRI-based tumor diagnosis. Further to investigate the contribution of LBP, Statistical analysis chi-square and p-value tests are used to confirm the significant impact of LBP feature space for identification of brain Tumor. In addition, The SHAP analysis was used to identify the most important features in classification. In a small dataset, CNN obtained 97.8% accuracy while SVC yielded 98.06% accuracy. In subsequent analysis, a large benchmark dataset is also utilized to evaluate the performance of learning algorithms in order to investigate the generalization power of the proposed model. CNN achieves the highest accuracy of 98.9%, followed by SVC at 96.7%. These results highlight CNN's effectiveness in automated, high-precision tumor diagnosis. Code: https://github.com/asifrahman557/BrainTumorDetection

infographic.key_insight: CNN and SVC achieved high reported accuracy in MRI brain tumor classification, with CNN performing best on the larger benchmark dataset.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support MRI-based tumor assessment, but these research results do not establish readiness for clinical use.
method: Compared six feature representations, including LBP, Gabor filters, wavelets, Fourier transforms, CNN features, and run-length matrices.
Evaluated k-nearest neighbor, random forest, SVC, probabilistic neural network, and CNN classifiers.
Used statistical tests to assess LBP features and SHAP to explain feature contributions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported accuracy was 97.8% for CNN and 98.06% for SVC on a small dataset, versus 98.9% and 96.7%, respectively, on a larger benchmark dataset.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report dataset sizes, patient-level splitting, or external clinical validation, limiting assessment of generalizability.
infographic.paper_title: Enhanced MRI brain tumor detection using deep learning in conjunction with explainable AI SHAP based diverse and multi feature analysis

title: Scalable Bayesian Gaussian Process Classification for Cancer Histopathology: Calibrated Uncertainty Under Distribution Shift
authors: Yunru Zheng, Wun Ting Chan, Sampras Dsouza, Zhenyu Hong
abstract: Reliable uncertainty quantification is essential for clinical deployment of cancer diagnosis models, yet neural networks and variational Gaussian process methods can produce overconfident predictions, particularly under the distribution shifts that arise when models trained at one hospital are applied at another. We present a scalable Bayesian Gaussian Process Classification (GPC) framework that operates on frozen pathology foundation model embeddings (Phikon) and combines accelerated Randomly Pivoted Cholesky (RPCholesky) for low-rank kernel factorization, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) with non-centered parameterization for posterior sampling, and a pivots-as-inducing-points scheme for prediction. This makes HMC posterior sampling in the low-rank latent representation tractable at N approximately 300,000 training points, enabling HC-based low-rank GPC on substantially larger datasets than prior MCMC-based demonstrations. We evaluate on two histopathology benchmarks for breast cancer metastasis detection: PCam and CAMELYON17-WILDS, where the latter tests calibration under hospital-level distribution shift. Compared to stochastic variational GP and neural network baselines, our method improves calibration and predictive performance - reducing expected calibration error by up to 88% and false negative rate by up to 90% - with the largest gains appearing under distribution shift, suggesting that HMC-based posterior sampling provides more trustworthy uncertainty estimates for cross-site pathology classification.

infographic.key_insight: A scalable Bayesian Gaussian process classifier improved uncertainty calibration and predictive performance in breast cancer histopathology benchmarks, with the largest gains under hospital-level distribution shift.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Better-calibrated predictions could support more reliable cross-hospital pathology AI, but benchmark results do not establish clinical safety or benefit.
method: Extract frozen histopathology embeddings with the Phikon foundation model.
Use accelerated RPCholesky for low-rank kernel approximation and selected pivots for prediction.
Sample the Bayesian posterior using non-centered Hamiltonian Monte Carlo at approximately 300,000 training points.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on PCam and CAMELYON17-WILDS reported up to 88% lower expected calibration error and up to 90% lower false negative rate versus stochastic variational GP and neural network baselines.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish prospective clinical performance or computational requirements for routine deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Scalable Bayesian Gaussian Process Classification for Cancer Histopathology: Calibrated Uncertainty Under Distribution Shift

title: Computation, not weight access: large language models as auditors of clinical prediction networks
authors: Zhiyu Liu, Xinyu Yang
abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) have been reported to read, edit and write the weights of small neural networks, raising the prospect of auditing clinical prediction models from their files alone. Public demonstrations, however, mixed reading raw weights with running code. We separated these conditions in internally pre-specified simulation experiments. Tanh networks of 105 to 38,401 weights were trained on simulated cohorts of patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage, each with a planted relationship or none, and one network was trained on labels that under-recorded deaths in a subgroup. GPT-6 Astra and four other GPT models answered single prompts under a default or an explicit system instruction, either with the weights in the prompt and no tools, or with a calculation-only tool that exposed the weights (white box) or only the network's predictions (black box). Without tools, Astra recovered planted relationships in 353-weight networks but became unreliable at 3,457 weights, and under the default instruction it declined 11 of 12 audit and repair tasks as unidentifiable; the explicit instruction removed these refusals. With the tool, it recovered the planted relationship in all 29 runs on networks of up to 38,401 weights, raised no false alarm in 15 runs on null networks, and found the biased subgroup in 6 of 6 runs. Black-box access performed as well as white-box access, and other GPT-6 models read as accurately. A well-designed script matched the comparator models on the audit and the best LLM repair. For auditing these networks, what mattered was computation and elicitation, not access to the weights.

infographic.key_insight: In simulated clinical prediction networks, reliable LLM auditing depended on computation and explicit instructions, not direct access to model weights.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Tool-assisted LLMs may help identify learned relationships and subgroup bias in clinical prediction models, but real-world clinical usefulness remains untested.
method: Trained networks with 105–38,401 weights on simulated subarachnoid haemorrhage cohorts with planted relationships or no relationship.
Compared five GPT models using raw weights without tools versus calculation tools with weight or prediction-only access.
Tested default versus explicit instructions, subgroup death under-recording, and a scripted comparator.
infographic.evidence_signal: With calculation tools, GPT-6 Astra recovered planted relationships in 29/29 runs, raised no false alarms in 15 null-network runs, and identified the biased subgroup in 6/6 runs; prediction-only access matched weight access.
infographic.watch_item: These simulation results do not establish clinical validity, and a well-designed script matched comparator-model audits and the best LLM repair.
infographic.paper_title: Computation, not weight access: large language models as auditors of clinical prediction networks

title: LLM-Assisted Label Noise Correction for EEG-Based Sleep Stage Classification
authors: Elmira Salari, Shruti Kshirsagar
abstract: Automatic sleep stage classification from electroencephalography (EEG) signals is a critical task in clinical sleep medicine. While deep learning models have shown promising results in this domain, their performance is fundamentally constrained by the quality of training labels, which human experts manually annotate and that are subject to inter-rater disagreement and systematic labeling errors. In this paper, we propose a novel LLM-assisted label-noise filtering pipeline that operates exclusively during training to identify and remove unreliable sleep-stage annotations before retraining the classifier. Specifically, TinySleepNet is first trained on the original dataset to extract per-epoch SoftMax confidence scores, then low-confidence epochs are submitted to LLaMA 3.1 along with their EEG spectral features and surrounding sequence context. The LLM evaluates each epoch against AASM sleep-scoring guidelines and assigns a verdict of RELIABLE or SUSPICIOUS. Suspicious epochs are removed from the training set, and TinySleepNet is retrained on the cleaned data. Evaluated on the Sleep-EDF Expanded dataset using 20-fold cross-validation, our method improves overall accuracy from 81.8% to 84.6% and Macro F1-score from 75.6% to 77.4%, with particularly notable gains in REM detection. Crucially, because the LLM operates only during training, the lightweight TinySleepNet architecture (1.3M parameters) is preserved at inference, making the proposed pipeline suitable for real-time, wearable sleep monitoring applications.

infographic.key_insight: Training-only LLM filtering of potentially unreliable EEG sleep-stage labels improved TinySleepNet classification without adding inference-time complexity.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support lightweight, wearable sleep-stage monitoring, though clinical utility remains unestablished.
method: Train TinySleepNet on original labels and flag low-confidence epochs.
Use LLaMA 3.1 to assess flagged epochs using EEG spectral features, sequence context, and AASM scoring guidelines.
Remove epochs judged suspicious and retrain TinySleepNet.
infographic.evidence_signal: On Sleep-EDF Expanded with 20-fold cross-validation, accuracy rose from 81.8% to 84.6% and macro F1 from 75.6% to 77.4%, with notable REM detection gains.
infographic.watch_item: Low-confidence epochs may include valid, difficult examples; the abstract does not report independent expert validation of the LLM's filtering decisions.
infographic.paper_title: LLM-Assisted Label Noise Correction for EEG-Based Sleep Stage Classification

title: From Natural Images to Medical Scans: Transferability of Diffusion Models for Medical Image Generation
authors: Efthymios Georgiou, Ioannis Kakogeorgiou, Sarah Brüningk
abstract: Transfer learning from natural images is standard in supervised and increasingly adopted in self-supervised medical image analysis, but its role in generative modelling, and in particular diffusion denoisers, remains underexplored. Medical diffusion models typically train the denoiser from scratch, with no systematic evaluation of natural-image transfer. We analyse this across latent and pixel paradigms, model sizes (131M-952M) and two radiology datasets (RadImageNet, BraTS), and ask which aspects of transfer support generation. We find that: i) Natural-image initialisation consistently improves generation, by 21-34% relative gFID in pixel space against 14% in latent space, where the tokeniser supplies much of the prior. gFID gains mirror downstream pathology classification and radiomic-feature FD, both proxies for clinical fidelity. ii) Benefits reflect spatial structure, not semantics: semantic probing does not predict generation quality, whereas a spatial-structure metric adapted to internal denoiser representations tracks gFID at $|r|=0.85$, positioning spatial organisation as a channel through which pretraining manifests. iii) Mixed-domain denoiser training shows that natural and medical images share similar layer-wise representations up to the late blocks, and mixing natural images into medical training improves fidelity. iv) Transfer benefit is tied to natural image initialisation, outperforming in-domain medical pretraining and several reinitialisation schemes. Overall, natural image denoisers transfer positively to medical ones in our setup. Code is available at https://github.com/CAIROLab-Bern/rad-dit

infographic.key_insight: Natural-image pretraining improved medical diffusion generation, with benefits linked to spatial structure rather than semantics.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Better synthetic-image fidelity may support medical imaging research, but the reported proxy improvements do not establish clinical utility or safety.
method: Compared natural-image initialization with training from scratch and alternative pretraining or reinitialization schemes.
Evaluated pixel- and latent-space diffusion models spanning 131M–952M parameters.
Probed internal representations and tested mixed natural–medical image training.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across RadImageNet and BraTS, natural-image initialization improved relative gFID by 21–34% in pixel space and 14% in latent space, with gains mirrored by pathology-classification and radiomic-feature evaluations.
infographic.watch_item: Results cover two radiology datasets and proxy fidelity measures; generalization to other settings and clinical use remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: From Natural Images to Medical Scans: Transferability of Diffusion Models for Medical Image Generation

title: Leakage- and Label-Aware Benchmarking of Class-Imbalance Strategies for Multimodal Chest X-Ray and EHR Classification
authors: Dang-Khoa Bui, Quang-Huy Tran, Minh-Khoi Nguyen-Bui, Duc-Tuan Ngo, Thanh-Trong Tran, Tuan-Khoi Nguyen
abstract: Benchmarks of class-imbalance strategies for multimodal chest X-ray (CXR) and electronic health record (EHR) prediction are often evaluated on record-level splits of cohorts in which one patient contributes several radiographs. We audit such a benchmark on 29,083 MIMIC-CXR radiographs of 10,479 patients with eight diagnosis targets. First, the record-split benchmark was misleading: a lookup table that copies the label of a development-set radiograph with the same EHR vector nearly matched the best model, and on unseen patients every model fell to the level of predicting every case positive. Second, tracing the labels back to MIMIC-IV explained why: each patient's labels are keyword matches on the diagnosis codes of a single admission, copied, with one EHR vector per patient, to all of the patient's radiographs, so about a third of the radiographs carry labels that differ from the codes of their own admission. Third, under patient-separated evaluation with admission-aligned and rule-refined labels, the initial conclusions do not hold: in the evaluated configurations no imbalance strategy raised the observed mean macro F2 over no augmentation by more than 0.01, tuned tree ensembles showed no consistent advantage over tuned logistic regression, and the released EHR variables stayed at the level of the all-positive baseline, whereas the diagnostic history available at imaging time and image embeddings exceeded it, including, with rule-refined labels, a CheXpert-trained encoder that never saw these radiographs; RAD-DINO had seen 96.6% of them during self-supervised pretraining. Adding either encoder to the diagnostic history gave no statistically significant F2 gain; exploratory AUROC gains were significant with RAD-DINO but not with DenseNet. We provide reusable diagnostics, a leakage-aware protocol and a checklist.

infographic.key_insight: Patient-separated, label-corrected evaluation overturned the benchmark’s conclusions: no tested imbalance strategy improved observed mean macro F2 by more than 0.01 over no augmentation.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Reliable assessment of multimodal chest X-ray models requires preventing patient overlap and aligning diagnostic labels with the relevant admission before considering clinical use.
method: Audited record-level splits using an EHR-based label lookup and unseen-patient testing.
Traced diagnosis labels to source admissions and evaluated admission-aligned, rule-refined labels.
Compared imbalance strategies, classifiers, diagnostic history and image embeddings under patient-separated evaluation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 29,083 radiographs from 10,479 patients with eight diagnosis targets, the lookup nearly matched the best record-split model, while every model fell to all-positive baseline performance on unseen patients.
infographic.watch_item: Encoder comparisons require pretraining-overlap checks: RAD-DINO had seen 96.6% of these radiographs during self-supervised pretraining.
infographic.paper_title: Leakage- and Label-Aware Benchmarking of Class-Imbalance Strategies for Multimodal Chest X-Ray and EHR Classification

title: Multimodal Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts for 3D Medical Vision-Language Modeling
authors: Gizem Mert, Szymon Płotka, Pedro R. A. S. Bassi, Wenxuan Li, Zongwei Zhou, Jarosław B. Ćwikła
abstract: Medical 3D scans and reports are inherently hierarchical, with diagnostic cues concentrated in specific anatomical regions across multiple levels of organization. Yet, most medical vision-language models ignore this structure and fail to focus on clinically relevant anatomy. We introduce MedHiVE, which combines hierarchical vision-language Soft Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) with contrastive learning to jointly model fine-grained anatomy and global scan context. To our knowledge, MedHiVE is the first framework to route both vision and text tokens through a two-level SMoE hierarchy organized by anatomical scale, coupling this with report-derived anatomy-level contrastive alignment for 3D medical imaging. This replaces the direct region-text alignment of statically pooled features and vision-only hierarchical routing of prior work with dynamic, slot-based cross-modal information flow across anatomical scales. MedHiVE operates via a two-level, learnable token-routing mechanism, where local image and text features are first routed through a local SMoE and then fused by a global SMoE into unified multimodal representations. Contrastive learning aligns both anatomy-level and global vision-language representations in a unified space. Pre-trained on 25,000+ CT scans with anatomical supervision, MedHiVE consistently surpasses 11 state-of-the-art methods across 6 datasets on 3 tasks: segmentation, classification, and detection, demonstrating the importance of hierarchical modeling. The code for MedHiVE is at github.com/szczurek-lab/MedHiVE.

infographic.key_insight: MedHiVE models anatomical hierarchies in both 3D scans and reports to learn aligned local and global representations.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Anatomy-aware representations could support medical image segmentation, classification, and detection, though clinical utility remains unestablished.
method: Routes image and text tokens through local and global Soft Mixture-of-Experts layers.
Uses report-derived anatomical supervision to align anatomy-level and whole-scan representations.
Combines hierarchical token routing with contrastive vision-language learning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Pre-trained on 25,000+ CT scans with anatomical supervision, MedHiVE reportedly outperformed 11 state-of-the-art methods across 6 datasets covering segmentation, classification, and detection.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report effect sizes or prospective clinical validation, limiting assessment of practical benefit.
infographic.paper_title: Multimodal Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts for 3D Medical Vision-Language Modeling

title: GTAFL: Addressing Test-Agnostic Long-Tailed Federated Learning in Medical Image
authors: Guangyu Chen, Jingyun Zeng, Hui Jiang
abstract: In healthcare, protecting patient privacy is crucial due to the sensitivity of medical data and its extensive accessibility. Federated Learning (FL) offers a decentralized and privacy-preserving training paradigm, making it an ideal solution for healthcare applications. A critical challenge in healthcare is that real-world medical data often exhibits long-tailed distributions in local and global views. Existing methods addressing long-tailed FL problem typically assume that the model will be evaluated on uniform test data distribution. However, practical test data in healthcare systems is often agnostic and unpredictable, leading to potential model failures in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we introduce a novel task termed Test-Agnostic Long-Tailed Federated Learning and propose GTAFL, a comprehensive framework to address this challenge. During the training stage, GTAFL employs adaptive re-sampling, expert classifier retraining, and self-supervised learning to correct biased classifiers and distorted feature spaces caused by long-tailed training distributions. During the inference stage, an ensemble mechanism combines retrained expert classifiers to handle test data with unknown distributions. Extensive experiments on CIFAR10 and two medical datasets manifest that our framework outperforms other state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at https://github.com/cgy-lavine/GTAFL

infographic.key_insight: GTAFL addresses long-tailed federated learning when both training data are class-imbalanced and test-time class distributions are unknown.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could make decentralized medical-image models more robust to changing disease-class frequencies across healthcare settings, though clinical benefit is not established.
method: Adaptive re-sampling and expert classifier retraining address class-imbalance bias.
Self-supervised learning targets distorted feature representations.
An inference-time ensemble combines retrained experts for unknown test distributions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports outperforming state-of-the-art methods on CIFAR10 and two medical datasets, without naming the medical datasets or providing numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Robustness to unknown class distributions in benchmarks does not establish performance under broader real-world clinical shifts.
infographic.paper_title: GTAFL: Addressing Test-Agnostic Long-Tailed Federated Learning in Medical Image

title: Comprehensive real-world utilization, treatment trajectories, and outcomes of immune checkpoint inhibitors across cancer types: the multicenter FAIR-ICI cohort
authors: Ha, L. T.; Ver Donck, F.; Bassez, I.; Oeste, C. L.; Vulsteke, C.; Delombaerde, D.; Hens, D.; Prenen, H.; Croes, L.; De Meulenaere, A.; Debruyne, P. R.; Verhaert, M.; Aspeslagh, S.; Brusselaers, N.; Verbiest, A.
abstract: BackgroundImmune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed cancer treatment, yet evidence on their utilization, treatment trajectories, and effectiveness in routine clinical practice remains limited. We characterized real-world ICI use and outcomes across cancer types using the multicenter FAIR-ICI cohort and explored differences between real-world and pivotal trial outcomes. MethodsWe conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults receiving ICIs across four Belgian hospitals. Structured and unstructured electronic health record data were harmonized using the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model (OMOP-CDM) and natural language processing. We evaluated overall survival (OS), time on treatment (ToT), time to next treatment (TTNT), ICI discontinuation (>12-week treatment gap without re-initiation), and post-discontinuation survival. OS was descriptively compared with pivotal trials, and prognostic factors were assessed using multivariable Cox regression. An interactive public dashboard was developed to enable exploration of cohort characteristics, treatment patterns, and outcomes. ResultsAmong 3,231 ICI-treated patients, 2,514 (77.8%) had metastatic disease. Among metastatic patients, 568 (22.6%) discontinued ICI without subsequent systemic therapy. Median post-discontinuation OS was 21.4 months (95% CI 16.5-37.2), with 49.1% alive at 24 months. ToT and TTNT were generally shorter than OS, particularly in melanoma (median OS 78 months; ToT 7 months; TTNT 26 months). Real-world survival was frequently less favorable than in pivotal trials. ECOG [≥]2 was associated with poorer OS than ECOG 0-1 (adjusted HR 2.18, 95% CI 1.82-2.60). In NSCLC patients receiving pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy, survival with ECOG 0-1 more closely approximated trial outcomes, whereas survival with ECOG [≥]2 was substantially poorer. ConclusionsReal-world ICI treatment trajectories extend beyond active treatment, with some patients experiencing prolonged survival after discontinuation. Differences between real-world and trial outcomes highlight the importance of patient characteristics, particularly performance status, when interpreting trial evidence in routine care. FAIR-ICI provides a scalable framework for evaluating real-world immunotherapy effectiveness, treatment trajectories, and future investigations of treatment-related toxicity. HighlightsO_LIFAIR-ICI studied 3,231 patients across four Belgian hospitals and provides an interactive dashboard for subgroup exploration. C_LIO_LIAmong metastatic patients, 22.6% stopped ICIs without subsequent systemic therapy, with 49.1% alive at 24 months after stopping. C_LIO_LITime on treatment and time to next treatment were generally shorter than overall survival. C_LIO_LIReal-world survival was frequently less favorable than in pivotal clinical trials. C_LIO_LIPoor ECOG performance status was strongly associated with shorter survival and may contribute to trial-real-world differences. C_LI

infographic.key_insight: In the FAIR-ICI cohort, survival could extend well beyond immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment, while real-world survival was frequently less favorable than in pivotal trials.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Performance status was important when interpreting outcomes: ECOG ≥2 was associated with poorer overall survival than ECOG 0–1.
method: Retrospective cohort of 3,231 adults receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors across four Belgian hospitals.
Structured and unstructured electronic health records harmonized using OMOP-CDM and natural language processing.
Evaluated survival and treatment trajectories, with descriptive trial comparisons and multivariable Cox regression.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 568 metastatic patients who discontinued ICIs without subsequent systemic therapy, median post-discontinuation survival was 21.4 months; ECOG ≥2 was associated with higher mortality across the analyzed cohort (adjusted HR 2.18, 95% CI 1.82–2.60).
infographic.watch_item: Retrospective observational data and descriptive trial comparisons cannot establish treatment effects or explain all differences between real-world and trial outcomes.
